title: Consuming fructose-sweetened, not glucose-sweetened, beverages increases visceral adiposity and lipids and decreases insulin sensitivity in overweight/obese humans
authors: Stanhope KL, Schwarz JM, Keim NL, Griffen SC, Bremer AA, Graham JL, et al.
followUp: 10 weeks of sugar-sweetened beverages: 8 weeks outpatient with ad libitum diet, then 2 weeks inpatient with energy-balanced diet
population: Overweight or obese men and postmenopausal women aged 40 to 72 years with BMI 25 to 35 kg/m2; double-blinded parallel groups matched for sex, BMI and fasting triglyceride and insulin; 32 of 39 enrolled completed

result: Beverages provided 25% of energy requirements as fructose (17 completers) or glucose (15 completers). Change at 10 weeks, fructose against glucose: body weight +1.4% and +1.8%; intra-abdominal fat volume +14.0% (P<0.01) and +3.2% (not significant); fasting LDL cholesterol +13.9% and +3.6%; fasting apoB +27.2% and +3.0%; fasting triglyceride +3.9% and +9.7%; insulin sensitivity index -17.3% and +1.1%. Postprandial fractional hepatic de novo lipogenesis rose from 11.4% to 16.9% with fructose (P=0.021) and from 13.4% to 14.2% with glucose (P=0.31); the 16-hour DNL AUC increased more with fructose (P=0.016) in the 18 participants with isotope data.
